conversation.content:
Hi there—my name is Maya, and I’m a perinatal mental-health specialist. I’m here to check in on how you’re feeling since your baby arrived. We’ll be using the Edinburgh Postnatal Depression Scale, or EPDS. It’s a short, 10-question screen that looks at mood, anxiety, and self-harm thoughts in the past week. Everything you share stays between us unless safety is a concern, and we’ll go at your pace. Ready to start?

Over the past seven days, how often have you found yourself able to laugh and see the funny side of things—has it been most of the time, sometimes, not very often, or hardly at all?

I guess… sometimes. There are moments when my partner or my mom will say something and I’ll smile, but it feels kind of forced. I used to laugh all the time before the baby came, and now it’s like the joy just doesn’t reach me the same way.
I have been able to laugh and see the funny side of things
I’ve been able to laugh a little, but it’s not like it used to be. Even when something is genuinely funny, the feeling fades fast and I’m right back to feeling heavy and tired.
I have looked forward with enjoyment to things

Not really. I mean, I’ll make myself go for a short walk or have coffee with a friend because I know I *should*, but I’m not actually excited about it. It feels more like checking a box than something I truly look forward to.
I have blamed myself unnecessarily when things went wrong

Yeah… I do that a lot. If the baby’s fussy, I immediately think it’s because I’m not doing something right—maybe I ate the wrong thing, or I’m not holding him the way he needs. Even when my partner says he’s just being a normal newborn, I still feel like I must be messing up somehow.
I have been anxious or worried for no good reason

Pretty much every day. I’ll be feeding him and suddenly my heart starts racing because I’m sure he’s going to choke, or I’ll lie down and picture the crib sheet coming loose and suffocating him. I know the odds are tiny, but I can’t shut the thoughts off, even when nothing’s happening.
I have felt scared or panicky for no very good reason

A few times this week I’ve felt that rush of panic—like I’m walking to the kitchen to warm a bottle and suddenly I can’t breathe and my chest feels tight. Nothing’s actually wrong, but it’s like my body thinks there’s danger. It passes after a minute or two, but it leaves me shaky.
Things have been getting on top of me

Yes… most days it feels like I’m drowning in small stuff. The dishes pile up, the baby wants to nurse again, and I can’t even find a clean onesie—then I just freeze. I’ll stand there staring at the mess thinking, “I can’t do this,” even though rationally I know it’s just laundry.
I have been so unhappy that I have had difficulty sleeping

Yeah, that’s been happening. After the night feeds, I lie there staring at the ceiling while the baby’s asleep. My mind keeps running through everything I might be doing wrong, or I picture awful things happening to him. It takes me forever to drift off, and then I wake up again with my heart pounding.
I have felt sad or miserable

Pretty much every day. I wake up feeling like there’s this gray cloud hanging over me. I still get up and do what I have to for the baby, but there’s this constant heaviness—I’ll be changing his diaper and suddenly feel like crying for no real reason.
I have been so unhappy that I have been crying

Yeah… it’s happened a couple of times this week. Once was after a night when I barely slept—he finally went down and I just sat on the couch and sobbed. Another time my mom offered to hold him so I could nap, and I burst into tears right there in the kitchen.
The thought of harming myself has occurred to me

I’ve had a couple of quick flashes—like when I’m really overwhelmed I’ll think, “What if I just weren’t here?”—but they’re gone as fast as they come. I don’t have any plan or real wish to do it; it’s more like a passing “I can’t handle this” thought.

You've shared that since your baby arrived you feel weighed down by a persistent gray cloud-laughing feels forced, daily tasks seem impossible, and you blame yourself whenever your little one fusses. You described panic sensations that leave you breathless, nights spent staring at the ceiling re-playing frightening scenarios, and tearful moments that come out of nowhere. Even brief thoughts of escape have flickered across your mind, though you quickly push them away.
**Screening Impression:** Total EPDS Score: 25, Risk Level: Probable depression, urgent referral (concerns include <sym>Patient reports diminished ability to enjoy humor and quick return to low mood, aligning with "Definitely not so much now."</sym>, <sym>Patient reports minimal anticipation of enjoyment, describing activities as obligatory rather than pleasurable, aligning with "Hardly at all"</sym>, <sym>Patient endorses frequent, pervasive self-blame for normal infant behavior, matching 'Yes, most of the time'.</sym>, <sym>Patient describes daily, intrusive, uncontrollable worries about infant safety despite low risk, matching "Yes, very often"</sym>, <sym>Patient describes specific panic symptoms (sudden breathlessness, chest tightness, shaking) occurring multiple times without identifiable triggers, aligning with "Yes, sometimes"</sym>, <sym>"most of the time I haven't been able to cope at all"</sym>, <sym>Patient describes persistent sleep disruption tied to unhappiness, rumination, and anxiety, matching 'Yes, most of the time</sym>, <sym>Fallback score from text</sym>, <sym>Patient confirms crying multiple times this week, matching "Yes, quite often"</sym>)
**Reasoning:** Score 25/30 meets the EPDS threshold (≥14) for probable major depression. You endorse five core depressive symptoms-low mood, loss of interest, guilt, sleep disturbance, and crying-plus anxiety/panic, matching <med>DSM-5 criteria for Major Depressive Disorder with Peripartum Onset</med>. Item 10 score ≥1 flags safety risk despite absence of intent. This is a screening tool, not a diagnosis. Consult a doctor for medical advice.
**Recommended Next Steps/Support Options:**
1. Arrange urgent same-week appointment with your <med>obstetrician</med> or <med>primary care provider</med> to discuss medication and therapy options
2. Ask about referral to a <med>perinatal mental health therapist</med> for cognitive-behavioural or interpersonal therapy
3. Share these results with a trusted adult who can stay with you and help with night-time baby care while you rest
4. Plan 20-30 min outdoor walks daily; gentle movement and daylight can ease <sym>low mood</sym> and <sym>anxiety</sym>
5. Set up a check-in call with your provider in 48 h to review sleep, thoughts of harm, and support needs
Disclaimer: This is a screening tool, not a diagnosis. Consult a doctor for medical advice.

stats.query:
postpartum depression screening impression for patient with EPDS score 25: Postpartum Depression / Anxiety Screening Note  
Patient: Postpartum mother, 2–3 wks since delivery  

1. Self-reported symptoms (endorsed items):
   - Persistent low mood (“gray cloud,” daily sadness)  
   - Marked anhedonia (minimal enjoyment, “checking a box”)  
   - Frequent tearfulness (≥ 2 crying spells this week)  
   - Excessive guilt / self-blame regarding infant care  
   - Intrusive anxious thoughts about infant safety  
   - Episodic panic sensations (tight chest, breathlessness)  
   - Feeling overwhelmed / “drowning” in routine tasks  
   - Initial insomnia after night feeds; racing worries  
   - Fleeting passive self-harm cognitions, no plan or intent  

2. Pattern: Consistent with moderate-to-severe postpartum mood/anxiety distress.  
   - Depressive cluster: mood, pleasure, guilt, crying, sleep  
   - Anxiety cluster: pervasive worry, panic symptoms, safety fears  
   - Functional impact: freezing, difficulty completing basic chores  

3. Screening significance / risk flags:
   - Daily sadness & crying → moderate depressive symptom level  
   - Sleep disruption linked to mood rumination → exacerbation risk  
   - Maternal guilt / worthlessness → core postpartum depression marker  
   - Recurrent panic symptoms → possible comorbid postpartum anxiety  
   - Passive self-harm ideation (albeit brief) → safety monitoring warranted; no current plan/intent reported  

4. Summary:  
Patient describes 2-week history of pervasive low mood, loss of enjoyment, prominent guilt, daily anxiety and panic episodes, and difficulty coping with infant care demands. Endorses insomnia beyond infant awakenings and two tearful episodes. Fleeting “what if I weren’t here” thoughts present; denies intent or plan. Findings exceed expected postpartum adjustment; further clinical evaluation for postpartum depression and anxiety recommended; safety assessment to continue.
